analysis.one_liner: Repeals an estate tax rule that blocked wealthy families from freezing the value of their estates.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Max Baucus with no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without a hearing or vote before the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1987 Congress wrote a rule into the estate tax aimed at 'valuation freezes' — a technique where a business owner shifts future growth of company value to their heirs now, while keeping control and paying tax on only the old, lower value. This bill would repeal that anti-avoidance rule entirely, letting large estates use freeze techniques again. The bill never advanced: it was sent to the Finance Committee, which took no action, and it expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy families who own businesses or valuable assets would gain, because they could once again restructure holdings so that future appreciation escapes estate tax. Estate planning lawyers and advisors would also gain, since freeze techniques are complex services they sell.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy estate owners and estate planners

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals section 2036(c) of the Internal Revenue Code and the amendments that created it in the Revenue Act of 1987 and the Technical and Miscellaneous Revenue Act of 1988, erasing the valuation-freeze rules from the estate tax [S3].

Under those rules, certain transfers where the transferor keeps a life estate are pulled into the taxable gross estate; the bill would apply the tax code as if those provisions had never been enacted [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal estate tax is paid only by the largest estates, so the direct cost of the repeal would fall on the Treasury through lost revenue, borne by taxpayers generally. Ordinary working people are not directly affected either way.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the rule reopens an avoidance channel: a family that owns a company can freeze its taxable value at a low point and shift all later growth to heirs free of estate tax, shrinking the estate tax base [S2].
The estate tax applies only to very large estates, so the bill's benefits would flow almost entirely to wealthy families rather than to ordinary taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits would go almost exclusively to families with large estates and to the professionals who structure their plans, while the cost is lost estate tax revenue that others must make up. There is little in the bill for ordinary working people.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Max Baucus introduced the bill on September 28, 1989 [S1].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance [S5].
The Finance Committee took no further action, and the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The estate-tax anti-freeze rule stayed on the books, so wealthy families and estate planners did not get the repeal they sought, and the federal estate tax base was not narrowed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The estate tax base; wealthy families lost the repeal

for.name: Sen. Max Baucus
for.role: U.S. Senator from Montana and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate tax valuation-freeze provisions and referred it to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: The Senate committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A Democratic senator sponsored the bill, no one else joined, and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan lineup appears in the record.

industries.note: Repealing the anti-freeze rule would restore demand for complex freeze transactions that these professionals sell to wealthy clients. The revenue those transactions shelter comes out of the federal estate tax.

industries.industry: Families owning large businesses and estates
industries.note: The repeal would let large estates restructure holdings so future appreciation avoids estate tax. Ordinary taxpayers are not directly affected, but the Treasury would collect less.
